speechtext:
I wish to lay on the table a copy of the treaty between the U.S.S.R. and the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland of alliance in the war against Hitlerite Germany and her associates in Europe and of collaboration and mutual assistance thereafter.
A copy of this treaty was to-day, I believe, tabled in the House of Commons of the United Kingdom. The government of Canada has sent the following message, through myself, to Mr. Churchill, the Prime Minister of Great Britain:

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF JOINT UNITED STATES AND UNITED KINGDOM BOARDS ON PRODUCTION, RESOURCES AND FOOD

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF JOINT UNITED STATES AND UNITED KINGDOM BOARDS ON PRODUCTION, RESOURCES AND FOOD
speechtext:
I promised my hon. friend the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Coldwell) that I would give him a brief statement to-day with respect to closer coordination of United Kingdom and United States production programmes, to which he made reference yesterday.
The Canadian government cordially welcomes the new arrangements for the closer coordination of the United Kingdom and United States production programmes, which were announced in Washington on June 9. The United Kingdom-United States combined production and resources board and combined food board should help greatly in the vitally important task of integrating, for war purposes, the productive capacities of both countries.
The Canadian food production programme has been geared to the needs of the war situation for two years now. From the outset of the war we have been proceeding on the policy that the entire food resources of Canada and the United Kingdom were in a common pool, about which the fullest information has been exchanged. We have, for example, been working for more than two years on a programme of increasing our bacon and cheese production to meet the United Kingdom's war requirements, and have been cutting down our domestic consumption of such essential products to make sure that the basic requirements of the United Kingdom were met. More recently, through the medium of the Canada-United States joint economic committees, the two governments have been working out a war-time agricultural programme under which each country can devote its energies to expanding the production of those farm products which it is best equipped to contribute to the common cause.
Similarly, in the field of industrial war production, Canadian capacity has been expanded and developed in the closest possible cooperation, first with the United Kingdom and now with the United States as well. Through the operations of the Canada-United

Questions
States joint war production committee and of War Supplies Limited, the efficient integration for war purposes of Canadian-American productive capacity has been making satisfactory progress. The new direct arrangements for formalizing a similar United Kingdom-United States relationship should help greatly in organizing the war effort of the united nations as a whole.
The task of working out suitable working arrangements for the effective cooperation of the united nations in the job of winning the war is still incomplete. The creation of the new boards announced this week marks a long step forward in the problem of organization. Through what agencies and representatives our existing cooperation with both the United Kingdom and the United States can most effectively be coordinated with the new United Kingdom-United States boards is receiving the consideration of the government.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF JOINT UNITED STATES AND UNITED KINGDOM BOARDS ON PRODUCTION, RESOURCES AND FOOD
speechtext: With the early part of the statement of the Prime Minister I am in agreement. But inasmuch as our food and munitions production in Canada has advanced from the low gear to the second gear stage-we hope that we are now working on all eight cylinders, and in high gear-are we to be left, with respect to these joint boards, with representation by a citizen of the United States, no matter how eminent or capable he may be? Surely Canada has arrived at the stature of a nation, and if there is to be representation it should be by a representative of this government. I am sure the Prime Minister will agree with that and insist upon that position.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF JOINT UNITED STATES AND UNITED KINGDOM BOARDS ON PRODUCTION, RESOURCES AND FOOD
speechtext: I certainly do not take any exception to what my hon. friend the leader of the opposition has said. All I would point out is that the agreement just concluded between the United States and the United Kingdom was reached within the past day or two. I have no doubt, having regard to our position and to the relationships that we have had both with the British government and with the United States government, that we shall be able to effect some arrangement in connection with food production along the line indicated by my [DOT]hon. friend.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS

speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, June 10, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mackenzie King for the second reading of Bill No. 80, to amend the National Resources Mobilization Act, 1940.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe the people of this country are anxious for a total war effort, including the compulsory mobilization of all our resources, both human and material. But total war must mean total war for everything and not only for human life. [DOT]
It is our view that political considerations have distorted the issues before the people and have unnecessarily divided our country. No section of our people, neither English nor French-speaking, has been told in clear and definite terms what we are fighting for, what the needs of the war are. Unreal and partisan political discussion has unfortunately made the question of conscription for overseas service the main issue. For some English-speaking Canadians it has become the symbol of total war; for most of our fellow-Canadians of the French language it has become the symbol of a surviving colonialism and an effort at domination to which they object. Thus, when unity in our country is a matter of life and death, we are rent by dissension and ill-will. More than that, not only the war but the post-war period is endangered by this disunity.
A large share of the responsibility for the present dissension lies squarely on the shoulders of the government. In time of acute crisis the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has been and still is pursuing his well known technique of procrastination in the hope that time will solve problems that cry for immediate solution. The result has been confusion and distrust, instead of understanding and confidence.
Even now the issue is being confused by the government. The people arq being told that the amendment before us does not introduce

Mobilization Act-Mr. Caldwell
conscription but merely frees the government's hands. Of course, I realize that the mere amending of the act does not of itself automatically abolish the voluntary system, but of what importance is that as compared with the paramount fact that this is the last opportunity which parliament has of declaring itself on the subject? If this amendment is passed, every restriction on the government will have been removed and the government will be free to impose conscription for overseas service at any time, on any terms it sees fit, and without any further reference to parliament. This is contrary to all the assurances of the Prime Minister that parliament would decide this issue.
I submit that nothing is gained and much harm is done by this new confusion. For who is satisfied by the government's interpretation of this amendment? No one. Those who want conscription are incensed by this policy. Those who are opposed to conscription do not believe it. And the result is still further confusion, further argument and discussion, prolonged controversy and increasing bitterness. This -lack of leadership, this policy of drift cannot be tolerated any longer. As I said in my broadcast during the plebiscite campaign, the "yes" vote was another indication that the people of Canada want a war policy which places all of the nation's resources at the service of the nation's cause-without profits, without special privilege, and without the evils of monopoly control. Amd, what is more, I am profoundly convinced that such a policy would greatly reduce the opposition to conscription for overseas service.
We deplore that conscription of man-power for overseas service has been allowed to take on such importance and to divide our people. For it is not the most vital issue facing this country to-day-and it certainly ought not to be a political issue. In our view, the problem of conscription for overseas service should not be dealt with on the basis of past prejudices and divisions. It is purely a question of strategy and should be considered exclusively on the basis of how we can make our best and most effective contribution to the defeat of the Hitler axis. We should think about it only in terms of our national interest and that of our allies, whose existence and freedom-as well as our own-depend upon the outcome of this war.
The Prime Minister yesterday asked parliament to free the government's hands so that it might by order in council adopt any policy which the war situation may make necessary. No man has more frequently assured this country that such policies would be decided
by parliament than the Prime Minister. Surely the government realizes that at no time since the outbreak of war has the situation been more critical than now. Everyone agrees that the campaigns of this year will decide the war. What should be done ought to be done now, with and by the consent and approval of this parliament. We have no right to give a blank cheque to the government to do nothing, or to make regulations for the conscription of man-power, which may be no better understood or more equitably administered than the regulations already in effect and about the meaning of which there is no general agreement by the Department of National War Services which is charged with their administration. Under the circumstances my colleagues and I do not propose to give the government a blank cheque to do by order in council what this parliament alone should do.
In my broadcast of April 21, I said of the issue of conscription: "The issue will be decided by parliament when and if the government presents it for discussion", and I insist that parliament and not the governor general in council shall decide the issue. The significant thing we have to face is that the controversy over the narrow issue now before the house has deeply-rooted causes-causes much deeper than the mere question of conscription for overseas. The divisions in our country to-day are the result of twenty-five years of political manoeuvring, and, added to this, the fact that throughout this period, in war as well as in peace, Canada has never pursued a foreign policy based on independent thought and judgment as befits a sovereign country. They arise from the fact that at no time has the government made clear to the people that we are in this war for our own survival and that we intend to play our proper part in the conduct of the war jointly with all other united nations, and not merely to be the appendix of any stronger power. They arise also from the fact that we have never stated clearly and unequivocally that so far as we are concerned and so far as the free peoples everywhere are concerned this is not an imperialist war, but on the contrary Canada stands now, and will stand when peace comes, to fight for [DOT]freedom for all the subject peoples, whether it be in India, Asia, Africa, Europe or elsewhere. We should state clearly our determination, in the words of the Vice-President of the United States Mr. Henry R. Wallace, that "no nation will have the God-given right to exploit other nations". There must be neither military nor economic imperialism.

Mobilization Act-Mr. Coldwell
Finally I believe that the opposition to overseas conscription is due, in part at least, to the evidence everywhere of gross inequality of sacrifice, to the fact that the wide powers which were given the government in the National Resources Mobilization Act have so far been used mainly to conscript labour, to freeze agriculture, and to conscript manpower for home defence. They have not been used to impose equal sacrifices on the privileged and to harness industry and wealth to an all out war effort according to a national war production plan and without strengthening the hold of private monopoly over the life of our country.
These, I believe, are the real causes of the differences existing in Canada to-day. If we are to achieve unity, both for an effective war effort and for successful reconstruction afterwards, we must introduce now a new and dynamic policy along the lines I have just indicated. Conscription for overseas service alone will not meet the requirements of our contribution, nor. I must add. will mere opposition to conscription serve the cause of unity and freedom. Every experience in this war- our successes as well as our reverses-has underlined the correctness and, if I may say so, the far-sightedness of the position which we took in this regard at the beginning of the war. It has always been clear that Canada's vital contribution in this war must be the supplying of implements of war and of foodstuffs, in view of our small population, our industrial and agricultural resources, and the comparative safety of our manufacturing units from destruction by the enemy. This does not mean that I am suggesting that Canada should not make her proper contribution in man-power to meet the enemy wherever it is strategically important to fight him. On the contrary, we are convinced that Canada should make her proper contribution on the battle front in the same way as on the industrial front. But I condemn as thoughtless and irresponsible demagogues those people who speak of this war only or mainly in terms of soldiers and more soldiers. I would lay it down as an axiom for our country that any policy which would tend to increase our fighting services at the expense of our industrial effort, at the cost of reducing the production of war materials, would be a wrong policy. What we need, what we have lacked and still lack, is a comprehensive plan of selective service for our material resources as well as for our man-power.
Almost two years ago the people of Canada submitted to a national registration. But it is an open secret to-day that a new inventory of Canada's labour power must be taken. The 
director of national selective service is still at work gathering information upon which to base any positive system for the allocation of man-power. The registration of two years ago is apparently of no value whatever except for calling up men for military service. This is an outrageous example of the total lack of planning which has dogged our war effort at every step. To-day, after almost three years of war, there are still unemployed, and layoffs in key industries. Only last Friday my colleagues the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) and for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) brought to the attention of the government lay-offs in a Montreal plant producing tanks, and in the Associated Aircraft plant at Malton. There are still instances of lack of equipment in our training camps. We are still in the dark as to the man-power capacity of Canada, and, at the same time that hundreds of trained and semi-trained mechanics are doing guard duty or drilling in the army, the director of national service warned us, on Monday, June 1, that we are already faced with a serious shortage of skilled labour.
I repeat what we of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation have said many times m this house and elsewhere: a complete allout war effort is essential to victory. This involves much more than conscription of manpower for military service, whether for home defence or for overseas. Not only justice but efficiency, not only morality but cold-blooded reality, demand conscription of war industry, of accumulated wealth and of financial institutions even more, much more urgently than the conscription of human life. The important thing to remember is that two years ago almost to a day the National Resources Mobilization Act, which the government now seeks to amend, was passed. At the insistence of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) parliament made dramatic haste and in three days the bill went through all its stages. Hon. members will remember that the Prime Minister scolded the house for taking even this short time to discuss a bill which gave the government sweeping, one might almost say dictatorial, powers. Listening to him at that time, a gullible person might have got the impression that one hour after the passage of the bill the whole machinery of the government would go into action to mobilize the country for total war. Such* gullibility perhaps deserved the disappointment which it later suffered. For this act could more properly have been called the human resources mobilization act. Apparently only human life is considered a national resource. Industry and *wealth remain private resources to be hired at a profit or borrowed at interest.

Mobilization Act-Mr. Coldwell
I want to make it clear that I do not desire for one moment to belittle what has been done. Obviously we are producing vast quantities of war supplies, and compared with the first months of the war we have made great strides, but it is my conviction that we can accomplish much more than we have done hitherto, and we cannot afford to lose any more time. It is our duty not only to help win the war some time but to help win it as soon as possible. Every month cut off the war means the saving of many thousands of human lives. From this point of view, therefore, what we have failed to do is scandalous, although what we have managed to do is substantial, and our failures have in my view been due to the fact that the powers given the government under the mobilization act have so far been used mainly for the regimentation of oui human resources.
Look at the record. We have conscripted men for home defence. We have frozen wages without placing any floor under them, so that industrial wages as low as 30 cents or 35 cents an hour are still being paid in many parts of Canada, particularly in the province of Quebec, and frozen at that level for the duration of the war. We have frozen farm labour without providing the farmer with the means of paying his labourer a decent wage. We have introduced measures which in effect almost- note, I say almost-prohibit strikes; yet we have done nothing to guarantee the workers the right to organize and bargain collectively. We have frozen prices, which is in principle a very good thing; but we have done almost nothing to protect the primary producer under the scheme. We have set up machinery for the regimentation of labour under the National Resources Mobilization Act, but without prior consultation with the workers.
Against this record on the human side, set up the profits still being made by corporations, the extent to which the economic effort is controlled by representatives of monopoly interests, the great luxuries still possible to those with wealth, the increasing power and resources being concentrated in the hands of a few, and you have some of the fundamental reasons why there is so much discontent and suspicion in the country to-day. As I have already said, we need a new and comprehensive policy, a policy which would utilize every resource for victory, which would plan our war production with a view to achieving the greatest possible output, without any regard for private interests, and which would provide a minimum standard of living and a scheme of social security for all our people. Such a policy would inspire our people with a vision
of the new world for which we are fighting this war. For this reason I move in amendment:
That all the words after "that" in the said motion, be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"this bill be not now read a second time, but that it be resolved that provision for the introduction of conscription of man-power for overseas service without specific proposals for the immediate use of the power conferred by section 2 of the act, to conscript war industry, financial institutions and accumulated wealth, does not meet the urgent need for total war, imposes further inequality of sacrifice, and is, therefore, contrary to the peace, order and good government of Canada."
There has been a widespread demand that we define exactly what we mean when we speak of conscription of industry and wealth. I shall endeavour to give the house a detailed outline of the immediate proposals we have in mind. Before doing so, however, there are one or two preliminary observations I should like to make.
I know that in many instances the question of what we mean by conscription of industry and wealth is asked honestly by people who really want to know the concrete proposals intended by this policy; but I also know that in some cases the question is asked by agencies which know perfectly well what is meant and which are trying to belittle the policy by confusing the simple issue with which it deals. It is significant that in almost every one of the many editorials written by newspapers on the subject recently, they say first that they do not know what conscription of wealth means, and then immediately go on to state that wealth has already been conscripted. They do not know what it means but it is already being done. I do not think I need point out further the obvious dishonesty of such criticism. I should like to make it clear that the proposals I am about to discuss are not exhaustive. They are the main, immediate steps which in our view are essential to an all-out war effort and to any policy approaching equality of sacrifice. The proposals we place before the government, parliament and the people are half a dozen concrete measures which I outlined in my speech to this house on January 26 of this year. I will enumerate them first and1 then deal with each one in turn. They are as follows:
1.	Nationalization of financial institutions, so that without inflation or accumulating debt we can finance our war effort.
2.	Compulsory, interest-free loans levied according to ability to contribute, as one of the means of war financing.
Mobilization Act-Mr. Coldwell

3.	Government ownership or complete control of all essential war industries so that every plant can take its place as a unit in a comprehensive national plan of war production.
4.	Replacing all dollar-a-year men by fulltime national administrators paid only by the state and working in conjunction with war boards on which labour and farm organizations are properly represented.
5.	A 100 per cent tax on all profits in excess of 4 per cent on capital actually invested, as has been suggested in our sister dominion of Australia.
6.	The establishment of a fair maximum-minimum income, a steeply graduated tax on incomes between the minimum and maximum, and a 100 per cent tax on all incomes above the maximum.
The proposals are complementary one to the other and should be taken as parts of a whole plan. In our view this is the only way in which we could in this country achieve the three simple objectives which the Hon. Walter Nash, former minister of finance of the New Zealand Labour government, placed before the select committee on reconstruction and reestablishment the other day. You will recall he emphasized three things:
1.	That no one who goes away from his country to fight ought to be worse off because he goes away to fight.
2.	That nobody ought to be better off because he stays at home.
. 3- That no one in the present world situation should at any time expect a profit from the supply of essential things associated with the war.
Since the government is seeking power for the final step in the conscription of man-power for overseas, now is the time to demand that these principles be put into effect. Moreover, the Prime Minister has lectured the house se\ eral times this session on the necessity of public men and political parties honouring their pledges and living up to their promises. On April 21 I appealed to the Canadian people to support the affirmative vote in the plebiscite.
* In making the plea I said:
I want to make it clear beyond the slightest chance of misunderstanding that we of the C.C.P. will not only continue hut will intensify our demand for the conscription of war industry, accumulated wealth and the financial institutions, on the same basis and at the same time as the compulsory mobilization of human power. To us, the value of the plebiscite lies only in the opportunity it gives our people of clearing away the underbrush of irrelevant argument. Once that is cleared away, the path to a total and just war policy will be open. We shall 
accept an overwhelming and united "yes" vote next Monday as another indication that the people of Canada are anxious for a war policy which places all the nation's resources at the service of the nation's cause-without profits, without special privilege, and without the evils of monopoly control.
Now let me deal with the relevance and meaning of each one of the proposals I have enumerated.
The first deals with the nationalization of the chartered banks. We of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation have always contended that the financial system should be publicly owned and operated for the common good. Hon. members will have noticed that one of the first controls which the government found it necessary to impose in this war was the control of foreign exchange. Banks are instruments of financial and investment policy. It is absurd to leave any portion of this policy in private hands during a crisis such as the present. I am not speaking of the profits made by the banks, although the nine chartered banks in 1941 recorded a total profit of over $13,000,000. The more important thing, however, is the control of policy, which should be exclusively in the hands of the government. Only in this way could we pursue a monetary policy which would be in harmony with the needs of war production and investment. In this way, too, we would have the full information about the monetary situation which is necessary for an intelligent policy.
But there is one additional reason why the public ownership of the chartered banks and government control of financial and investment policy is of great interest at the present time. Everyone is aware of the important part which these factors played in the prewar years. These factors will be equally crucial in the reconstruction period after the war. It will be necessary for the country as a whole collectively to control and direct investment and to finance huge schemes of public enterprise.
Some time ago the Prime Minister correctly stated in a public address that unless we lay the foundations of the new world order during the war we may look for it in vain. The right hon. gentleman was right. I now call upon him to implement his words, since he and he alone has the full power to direct the policy.
One final word on the question of banks. I hope no one will raise the bogey about such a step as I am urging disrupting our war effort. Banks do not produce anything. They could not produce a contraption which would shoot a pea at Hitler, let alone a gun, a tank or a plane. They might however harm our war effort by anti-social policies.

Mobilization Act-Mr. Coldwell
The second proposal we make is that when it is necessary for the state to borrow money from individuals and corporations it should be by means of interest-free loans to be levied on a graduated scale according to ability to subscribe. This is of crucial importance. Hon. gentleman will recall during the twenty years between the two wars the public treasury paid millions of dollars in interest charges. According to the figures published in appendix "A" to the Sirois report, page 41, the net annual debt charges of the dominion grew from $12,213,000 in 1913 to $152,488,000 in 1921, an increase of more than 1,200 per cent as a result of loans made in the last war. The loans which we have made in this war are already tremendously larger than those of the last war, although the rate of interest is lower. And we are not finished yet. What will this mean when the war is won? The same thing that it meant in the past: public works, programmes of social service, the needs of our people for education, for homes, for safeguarding health and providing for their old age-all will suffer because the cry will be raised that contractual obligations are sacred. Consequently the major share of the national revenue will be paid out in interest.
I declare that this is immoral. Do we promise interest in perpetuity to our young men whom we send to give their lives for this country and for the cause of freedom? Early in this war the President of the United States had the wisdom and generosity to introduce the lease-lend arrangement so as to avoid crippling the post-war period through international debts. We ourselves have made a free gift of 81,000,000,000 to Britain. Yet when we need the financial resources lying unused in Canada we pay interest on them now and forever more. "Profitable patriotism," the late Mr. Lapointe called it. Unpatriotic extortion would be more nearly correct.
There is a bogey in connection with this proposal which should be laid immediately. We are asked: Are you threatening to take the savings of the poor widow and the orphan? I wish many of them had savings; I am certain they would be among the first to offer them to our cause in this war. No; we are threatening no such thing. You will have noticed that we say that compulsory interest-free loans should be levied on a graduated scale according to ability to subscribe. The small savings of individuals which are meant for a rainy day, for possible ill-health or similar needs, should be exempt.
Then we are asked: What about the subscriptions of such institutions as life insurance companies, whose earnings are widely distributed among small policyholders? I am
certain every Canadian would gladly forego the small sum which he receives in dividends on his policy each year if by doing so he could be guaranteed social insurance against unemployment, bad housing and chaos after the war. This is precisely what in part the elimination of interest payments on war loans would mean.
The third proposal we make is either government ownership or, where that is not feasible, complete government control of all war industry. Tied in directly with this is the next proposal, that dollar-a-year men should be replaced by national administrators paid exclusively by the state, and that labour and farm organizations be given a proper share in the control of war production. I discuss these points together, since they concern one subject.
Production is still our main job in this war. Upon our success in this field depends our main contribution to victory. On many previous occasions my colleagues and I have pointed out the shortcomings in our war production and the utter lack of over-all planning. In fact it is true to say that the Department of Munitions and Supply has so far been merely a procurement department- It has sought to fill orders requisitioned by our own service departments or those of our allies. There has been no evidence of comprehensive planning to expand our war production to the maximum of our resources without affecting the health, efficiency and morale of our people. "Cost plus" contracts have been entered into. I understand that several hundred have been made. Private business has been allowed to bargain and haggle, to hinder necessary expansion, to continue to produce luxury articles requiring indispensable war materials, to influence our whole production policy by competitive considerations. Look at the record. Only a few months ago did we stop the production of pleasure automobiles, and it is not very much longer since we stopped production of other luxury articles, such as radios and refrigerators. Now we are short of rubber and steel and other materials which went into the manufacture of these articles during more than two years since the war began. In fact the years 1940 and 1941 were banner years for the automobile industry. Yet they were years during which France fell and Britain was on the brink of defeat, years during which the war became a world conflict and the cause of freedom became more and more dependent on contributions of this continent.
Some of the evils of the first two years have been corrected through the pressure of events. But we still have far too much "business as

Mobilization Act-Mr. Coldwell
usual," far too much tenderness towards private interests; still no plan based on a full inventory of our resources. I have already referred to layoffs which have occurred in Hamilton and Malton. The other day I drew the attention of the house to the possibility of oil deposits on Manitoulin island. These possible deposits of one of the most valuable resources needed for war are not even being investigated, because in 1909 a private lease was granted to an individual and corporation. In war at least such resources must belong to the people, to the nation, to the allied cause; private interests must not stand in the way of the national objective of victory.
As I speak, the Dumart packing plant in Kitchener is shut down. For almost four weeks the plant has kept the workers locked out, because they walked out for one hour in protest over the unfair dismissal of two of their fellow workers. The federal labour department and the provincial minister of labour have sought a settlement. The company says no; it will open the plant only on its own conditions, namely, that they take back whomsoever they like, and fire the most active unionists. The union has sent a brief to the Prime Minister asking him to send a controller to the plant, but that the government refuses to do. Think of it. In spite of the great need for bacon and similar meat products in Great Britain. In spite of the beef shortage at home, a private meat packing company is at liberty to shut down its plant for four weeks, to keep about three hundred men and women idle and in want- all because of the determination to block the union. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) does not act.

speechtext:
I could cite many more examples of the past and present. It is a simple statement of fact that our conversion to war production has been slow and tardy; that it has been impeded by considerations of the competitive position of private monopolies 
both now and after the war; that private business has been and still is allowed to control the effort within wide limits; that we have not had any comprehesive plan of war production based on the compulsory selective use of all our resources. And this in a war in which supplies and equipment mean the difference between victory and defeat. The united nations do not lack men. They do need, and need urgently, more and ever more equipment and supplies. To the extent that any private consideration is allowed to stand in the way of war production, to that extent do we betray our sacred obligations to our country and to our allies in this war.
Therefore we say that all war industry should be fully conscripted immediately. It would probably be difficult to acquire immediate public ownership of some industries without interrupting production, and we recognize that production must not be interrupted. But it is possible, without any difficulty, to say to private industry that for the duration of the war, its plants, its policies, its management are completely at the disposal of the nation, precisely in the same way as we have, without hesitation, said to the men and women of Canada that certain of them must place their lives at the service of the country; that others must for the duration of the war work where they are told, at a wage which may not be increased.
Another reason why our economic controls have not worked satisfactorily is that they have been in the hands of men who exclusively represent big business and continue to draw their salary and incomes from the corporations in which they have an interest. It is an accepted principle, though sometimes evaded in practice, that one who becomes a minister of the crown should thereupon sever whatever connections he may have had with private corporations. But our dollar-a-year men have almost as much legal power and a great deal more economic power than members of the cabinet, and should be subject to the same rule. Even if our big industrialists and financiers were angels-and the social history of our country show's some of them to have been far removed from the incorruptible inhabitants of heaven-they would still be the victims of divided loyalties and of the pressures of long-established ties and habits. Therefore we say that dollar-a-year men should be replaced by administrators who are employed by the state at a salary, and who are forbidden to receive any remuneration from private corporations.
Finally, on this question of production and control, it is absolutely essential that labour and farm organizations be properly represented

Mobilization Act-Mr. Coldwell
on all war boards. This is a war for democracy. The workers have no axe to grind other than the one needed to destroy Hitler and Hitlerism. Their zeal, their intelligence, their daily experience should be harnessed through giving them a share in the responsibility of planning and controlling production. In this way greater efficiency could be achieved, a feeling of confidence, selfrespect and responsibility instilled into our people, and a measure of democracy introduced into our war effort. Ernest Bevin has wisely said:
This talk of winning the war means you have to call for the utmost ingenuity you can get from the people, for every ounce of ability they have, for the willingness and courage to take decisions, to make them indifferent to enemy action and carry on. I do not believe you can do that with orders from the top.
In Canada we have taken no account of this important fact. It is only after almost three years of continuous pressure by us and by the labour unions that the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) has at last condescended to favour labour-management committees. Much more than that is needed. At the bottom there must be union recognition and collective bargaining, and then organized labour should be represented in the top councils as well as in plant committees.
The fifth proposal I enumerated earlier is to limit net profits to 4 per cent on capital actually invested. There is no reason why such a policy should not become immediately the law in Canada. It may well be argued that even 4 per cent is far too generous; that in a war such as the present, with so much at stake, no profits whatever should be made out of the production of war supplies. Again we are prepared to recognize the compromise which may be necessary in order to maintain continuous production. But 4 per cent is an adequate return. No business should demand more in this crisis.
An attempt has been made to foster the idea that the excess profits tax has really eliminated profits. I am quite prepared to admit that it has prevented the kind of profiteering which was known in the last war. But huge profits are still being made. The Financial Post for May 30 carries an analysis of the profits made by 146 selected companies. The final showing is that the 1941 net profits of these companies was 8-1 per cent higher than those of 1940 and 2-8 per cent higher than those of 1939. The Financial Post, as may be expected, draws the smug conclusion that this shows that profits are reasonable. Such a conclusion is without foundation. For any increase 44561-206
whatever over 1939 and 1940 is scandalous. The 1939 profits were for all industry, with the exception of the railways, among the highest since the last war. To allow in the second year of this war net profits-after all taxes greatly increased depreciation, inventory and other reserves-greater than those of one of the most profitable pre-war years is to make a mockery of the principle of equality of sacrifice. In fact, if the Financial Post had, as it should have, compared the 1941 profits with the average made in 1936-39-the basic period under the Excess Profits Tax Act-the 1941 increase would have been very substantially greater.
I have in my hand two tables: one of twenty-three companies which in 1941 made profits up to 30 per cent higher than the average made by the same companies for the basic period 1936-39; the other listing twenty-six companies whose 1941 increase over 193639 was 30 per cent or over. The aggregate increase in the first instance was 14 per cent over 1936-39 and 9 per cent over 1940. The aggregate increase in the second group was 62 per cent over 1936-39 and 29 per cent over 1940. I do not propose to take time to read them, but if it is desired, I shall be glad to place these tables on Hansard.

No, it would not carry a guarantee of 4 per cent. I know it will be said that it would not be possible with a 4 per cent return for an industry to build up a reserve to meet post-war conditions, but if everybody was limited to 4 per cent after allowing fair depreciation for different types of industry, I think that would be fair.
The apologists for the monopoly interests and big business point to the increased production and increased capital investment as justification for the increased profits. But what is responsible for the present production and who laid out the added capital expenditure? What right has private monopoly to extort a return on production for which it does not even have to advertise, production which is caused by a world calamity? And do not let us forget .that well over half a billion dollars have been invested by our government and that of Britain in the capital expansion made necessary by the war.
The important point in all this is not only the amount of money involved; it is the distortion of the purposes of this war which the situation reveals. It is the suspicion which



Mobilization Act-Mr. Coldwell
is engendered in people's minds. It is the principle of the thing, the injustice and inequality of sacrifice. If we ask young Canadians to submit to another step in the total conscription of their lives, then profits should at least be limited, if not eliminated.
Finally we propose the setting up of a minimum and maximum income and a tax beginning with the minimum and graduated steeply until it is 100 per cent for everything above the maximum. The minimum suggested is that of our present income tax law- $750 for a single man and $1,500 for a married person. As for the maximum I would suggest an amount between $12,000 and $15,000. The President of the United States suggested $25,000 for that country. In New Zealand they have established a maximum of $12,000. Fifteen thousand dollars would therefore seem to be a proportionate amount for Canada. I want to make it clear that the maximum would not be net, but would remain subject to income tax. Now that this parliament has exclusive powers in the income tax field, such a proposal can be conveniently carried out.
It is scandalous and inhuman that we should refuse to increase the miserly benefit now being paid the aged, that we should refuse even to give them the cost of living bonus. It is equally scandalous that we should, even now with maximum employment, have thousands of people living in slums and in bad health.
Our treatment of soldiers' dependents is equally deplorable. Many of them are partly dependent on the generosity of private organizations. Imagine the morale which can be instilled into these people whose breadwinners have gone to give their lives for their country; yet they must depend on private charity to live in decency. Faith in the war, unity among our people for victory, zeal in production-all these indispensable assets of a people at war in a righteous cause, depend upon just and humane treatment of the masses of the people. We must give them something to defend and fight for. And we must show them that in this war no one in the land is allowed an income of excessive luxury.
. These are the concrete proposals which we have in mind under a policy of conscription of industry and wealth. I have dealt with them in considerable detail so that no one can hereafter say that they do not know what is meant. I appeal to hon. members to consider this policy on its merits. The time is overdue when we should attain a real total war effort and begin to lay the outlines of the just Canada which we should build after victory.
It is my conviction that such a policy would fire the imagination of all our people, would

make clear our objectives in the war and would win the unqualified support of every section of our people for any and every service which may be necessary. Remember the profound homely truth which the VicePresident of the United States enunciated recently:
The object of this war is to make sure that everybody in the world has the privilege of drinking a quart of milk a day.
Let us plan for this objective in our own country now. If an effective policy of conscription of industry and wealth were introduced now, we believe any restriction on military conscription could justly be removed and we would support it. But the government is not doing anything of the sort. In all respects it will continue the disastrous policy which it pursued until now. It only asks to be free to continue one step further the conscription of human life. The demands of the workers, the pleading of the farmers, the entreaties of the aged, the veterans, the sick and the dependents of the nation's heroes cannot move the government one inch towards greater democracy or justice or total economic conscription. But the shouts of reactionary super-patriotism for human conscription are immediately answered. We cannot and will not agree to giving of further powers for human conscription without concrete measures for the conscription of material resources.
This war, with everything which is at slake in it, with the heroism of whole peoples to inspire us, should have been the occasion for building a deeper unity in our own nation than we have ever known. That the contrary should face us now is a condemnation of the leadership and policies which have guided us since the outbreak of hostilities. I believe the policies which I have outlined could win back that unity, could build this nation into a powerful instrument for victory in the war and for a people's peace afterwards. That is why we urge them at this time.
